title: Leading Across Operating Systems
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Written with Andrew Barban, this piece argues that much cross-generational friction at work is not a clash of values but a clash of default behaviours formed in different economic and managerial climates. The opening scene of a fast responder and a careful responder to the same chat message shows how each reads the other through their own rules for what respect looks like. The authors draw on sensemaking, media richness theory, attention residue and feedback research to explain why professionalism, urgency and feedback are so easily misread. They reject generational stereotyping and propose a three-layer map of values, interpretations and protocols, with leaders intervening mainly at the protocol layer. Their example is separating acknowledgement from delivery with a simple response-time agreement. The payoff is a team that treats difference as coverage, combining institutional memory with momentum.
points: Conflict between cohorts often looks like a values dispute when it is actually different risk-management strategies shaped by the conditions in which people learned what good work looks like.
Leaders should separate values (shared), interpretations (where conflict hides) and protocols (explicit ways of working), and work mainly on the protocol layer where alignment is achievable.
Separating observable behaviour from assumed intent, and surfacing alternative readings, turns snap judgments about tone into something a team can discuss.
Explicit norms such as acknowledging within 30 minutes but delivering later stop people inferring character from response time and can be revisited without shame.
Mixed-cohort teams are an asset when their strengths are made interoperable, pairing judgement and institutional memory with adaptability and iteration.
quotes: These striking differences show when people bring different “work operating systems” into the same room, and is especially common when individuals are separated by decades. Our defaults are naturally shaped by the conditions in which we learn what “good work” looks like: the economic climate when we enter the workforce, the management fashions that reward certain behaviours, the tools available for coordination and the social norms around authority, identity and risk.

When different defaults collide, the mismatch can sound like a values conflict even when both sides want the exact same outcomes. This is a case where leadership has to pursue integration, by helping the team see these hidden default assumptions and developing a shared way of working.

For some, professionalism means restraint: a measured tone, fewer messages and a preference to resolve uncertainty before speaking. For others, professionalism is visible coordination: sharing early, updating often and using lightweight exchanges to reduce uncertainty together. Neither is inherently superior; each simply optimises for different risks.

The most useful move a leader can make is to separate what’s genuinely non-negotiable from what’s easier to misread. In cross-cohort teams, people often argue at the wrong level: they defend behaviours as if they were values, and they treat preferences as if they were principles.

Layer 3: Protocols. Protocols are the integration layer: the explicit rules of engagement that convert our own private assumptions into expectations we can share with team members and colleagues (if you want to be less formal, you can call these ‘ways of working’). When protocols are clear, people don’t have to infer intent from behaviour nearly as much, and that is where a lot of resentment evaporates.

Treating cross-cohort collaboration as an integration challenge changes the nature of the work. The leader stops asking the team to “be more understanding” (which is vague and rarely actionable) and instead asks a concrete question: What do we need to make explicit so we can move with less friction?

Most importantly, an integration mindset turns the differences between cohorts from a liability into a form of coverage. People who have worked through different cycles tend to be good at anticipating second-order risks, spotting patterns and protecting quality under pressure. People who have grown up with the latest tools and norms tend to be good at adaptability and have more appetite for iterative coordination.
